lines: Avery Brooks
+1 (555) 010-3319 | avery.brooks@example.com | example.com/in/abrooks
Date of birth: 9 Jan 1998 | Nationality: Brazilian
EDUCATION
Eastmoor University | B.S. in Statistics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2016 - May 2020
EXPERIENCE
Pinecrest Insurance | Junior Analyst | Metro City, USA | Jul 2020 - Jul 2022
- Owned the claims backlog report and the weekly numbers the claims managers used.
- Analyzed 18 months of call-center data; my findings moved two agents to the evening peak and cut average hold time from 9 to 5 minutes.
- Wrote the team's SQL style guide and review checklist, which cut query errors found in review by half.

- Automated the monthly fraud-flag extract while also maintaining the team calendar, answering ad hoc questions from sales, updating onboarding documents and covering the help desk on Fridays, which saved the fraud team 10 hours a month.
Brightcart Retail | Data Analyst | Metro City, USA | Aug 2022 - Jun 2025
- Improved reporting efficiency by 90% by moving the monthly revenue report to scheduled SQL queries.
- Found customers with no orders by left-joining the orders table to the customers table and counting rows with a null customer name.
- Wrote data-quality checks on the 40 most-used tables, catching 15 broken loads before they reached a dashboard.
- Presented the quarterly customer review to the leadership team, and two of its three recommendations were funded in the next budget.
- Reported the national conversion rate as the simple average of 14 regional conversion rates, without weighting by regional traffic.
- Built the weekly retention dashboard for 2.4M customers that marketing used to retarget lapsed buyers, lifting 90-day repeat purchase from 22% to 27%.
PROJECTS
City Bike-Share Demand Study | Independent Project | Python, SQL | Jan 2025 - Present
- Modeled hourly bike-share demand for 120 stations from 2 years of public trip data, forecasting next-day demand within 12% mean absolute error.
- Compared the forecast with the operator's rebalancing schedule: empty-station hours fell from 310 to 205 a week in a replay of last summer.
- Published the notebooks and a short write-up, which the city's open-data team linked from its bike-share page.
Food Pantry Visit Analysis | Volunteer, Team of 3 | Excel, SQL | Mar 2023 - Aug 2023
- Mapped 14 months of pantry visits by hour and day, so the pantry moved one volunteer shift and cut the Saturday line from 50 to 20 minutes.
- Cleaned 9,000 handwritten visit logs into a single table and matched repeat visitors, giving the pantry its first count of unique households.
- Built a retention dashboard for about 2.4 million shoppers that raised repeat purchases by nearly a quarter.
SKILLS
Tools: SQL, Python, Excel
Methods: dashboards, forecasting, metric design, data-quality checks

items.says: The résumé includes date of birth and nationality details that readers are not meant to weigh.
items.because: They are not relevant to judging analyst experience and use space that could go to qualifications.

items.says: The experience entries are not ordered newest first.
items.because: Pinecrest appears before the more recent Brightcart role, interrupting the expected reverse-chronological scan.

items.says: Work history should appear before education.
items.because: The candidate has several years of analyst experience.

items.says: The bullet states responsibility for the report without showing the reporting work.
items.because: The responsibility framing leaves the analytical or reporting skill unclear.

items.says: The bullet does not show what the weekly numbers helped managers accomplish.
items.because: A reader cannot see what managers did with the numbers or what changed as a result.

items.says: The staffing-change analysis is described only in general terms.
The bullet uses a first-person pronoun.
The strongest call-center result is not the opening line of the entry.
The fraud-automation result is buried in a list of unrelated support duties.
items.because: The time saving follows several tasks, obscuring which work produced it and making the accomplishment read like a task list.

items.says: The 90% improvement is not tied to a defined measure.
items.because: A reader cannot tell what “reporting efficiency” measures, making the percentage hard to interpret or assess.

items.says: The two uses of “by” make the result-and-method relationship awkward to scan.
A null customer name does not reliably identify customers with no orders.
items.because: A customer may have a null name even when an order matched in the join.

items.says: The finding about customers with no orders lacks a scale or a stated consequence.
items.because: Without the group’s size or what the finding informed, its practical value is difficult to judge.

items.says: The bullet does not identify what kind of data-quality check was used.
The simple average of regional conversion rates is not the national conversion rate when regional traffic volumes differ.
items.because: An unweighted average gives each region equal influence rather than reflecting conversions and traffic across all regions.

items.says: The conversion-rate report has no stated consequence or concrete reported result.
items.because: A reader cannot see what the reporting mattered for.

items.says: The strongest result is at the end of the entry rather than leading it.
The Brightcart entry’s topics lack a clear progression.
The bullet does not name the forecasting approach.
items.because: A reader cannot see the technical method behind the forecast.

items.says: The bullet does not establish what the 12% error is relative to.
items.because: The percentage error has no stated basis or comparison, making predictive performance difficult to assess.

items.says: The forecast-accuracy result appears after the station count and data period.
The strongest project outcome is not the first project bullet.
“Which” does not make clear whether the notebooks or the write-up were linked.
The pantry outcome comes after a long explanation rather than leading the project entry.
items.because: A scanning reader reaches the shift change and shorter Saturday line only after the “so the pantry” clause.

items.says: The unique-household result is wordy.
items.because: The 9,000 logs describe the amount of data processed, not the result of matching repeat visitors.

items.says: The bullet does not give the unique-household count.
items.because: Without the count, the new result remains difficult to judge.

items.says: The shopper-retention claim duplicates the Brightcart achievement and does not describe a pantry outcome.
items.because: Repeating nearly the same achievement makes its attribution inconsistent and the pantry entry less credible.

items.says: The “nearly a quarter” increase has no stated comparison.
items.because: A reader cannot tell what the increase is measured against, leaving its size and meaning unclear.

items.says: The bullet does not explain how the dashboard informed the reported increase.
items.because: The connection between the deliverable and the claimed outcome is unclear.
